Half the world is ageing faster than any society in recorded history. The other half is still overwhelmingly young.

4 maps that explain the great demographic split — a thread 🧵🗺️

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)

1/ Map one: median age — the age that splits a country into two equal halves. Dark blue is old: Japan, Italy, Germany, South Korea and now China sit at or above 40. The palest countries in the Sahel sit under 20.

2/ The extremes barely look like the same species of society. Monaco's median age is roughly 54 and Japan's roughly 50. The Central African Republic and Niger are under 16 — half their people are children or teenagers.

3/ Map two: old-age dependency — people aged 65+ for every 100 of working age. Japan is above 50. Much of sub-Saharan Africa is under 6. A tenfold gap in who is supporting whom, on the same planet, in the same year.

4/ Map three: natural population growth. The orange band is the story. Across Europe, Russia, China, Japan and Thailand, deaths now outnumber births — these populations only hold steady, where they do, through migration.

5/ Map four: urbanisation, part of the mechanism. City families have historically had fewer children, and humanity crossed the 50% urban line around 2007. Roughly 57% now live in urban areas, up from about 30% in 1950.
6/ None of this reverses quickly. A country with a median age near 50 cannot become young again in a decade, whatever policy it adopts — the children who would have done it were never born.

7/ The most consequential map of this century may have nothing to do with borders. It's about age.

Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
